subject: Private deploy (VPC/on-prem) — keystore custody, subprocessors, and cross-border flow

Subject: Private deploy (VPC/on-prem) — keystore custody and data flows

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for the demo last week. We're evaluating Redwood for an EU on‑prem deployment (air‑gapped option). A few compliance questions came up from legal and our CISO: 

- Can customers retain sole custody of the master keys (KMS) in the on‑prem package? Any mandatory Redwood escrow or operator key access?
- What subprocessors (if any) would have network or log access to the deployment? We need a list and purpose scope for our DPA.
- Cross‑border export: will any telemetry or model artifacts ever leave the customer's network if we choose the fully private option?

If you can send a short summary and suggested DPA clauses we can share with Raj and procurement. Happy to hop on a call — but starting with a written playbook will speed internal approvals.

Thanks,
Anna Lopez
Head of IT Compliance
MedTech Health

Hi Anna — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Monica (Solutions) and Vivek (Legal) so we can provide both the technical playbook and DPA language.

Quick summary up front: for our fully private (VPC/on‑prem) option customers can keep exclusive custody of root/master keys with no Redwood operator access by default. We offer an optional key escrow workflow for customers that want Redwood‑assisted disaster recovery — that is never mandatory and is gated through explicit contract language and an operator break‑glass addendum.

Monica and Vivek, can you review and add the following into a single package: 1) short keystore custody playbook for on‑prem installs (what we ship vs customer‑managed), 2) suggested DPA redlines around subprocessor access and telemetry, and 3) confirmation of cross‑border guarantees (logs/metrics vs model weights). I'll attach our playbook and a first pass of DPA clauses in my follow up.

Anna — attaching the on‑prem keystore playbook and a draft DPA clause doc for initial review.

Subject: Re: Private deploy (VPC/on-prem) — technical scope and subprocessors

Anna / team — technical notes from Solutions (condensed):

1) Keystore options (on‑prem):
   - Customer‑managed KMS (recommended): customer generates and stores master key in their HSM/KMS. Redwood runtime is configured to accept keys via an encrypting keystore connector; we never persist the unwrapped master key.
   - Customer‑managed + optional escrow: customer can opt into an encrypted escrow held in an air‑gapped Redwood vault; access requires a documented break‑glass procedure and legal approval.

2) Operator access:
   - Standard: No operator root key access; our op engineers can only see anonymized telemetry and aggregate health metrics if allowed.
   - Emergency: Operator break‑glass only with documented justification, two‑party approval, and fully audited session recording. This is an addendum in the contract.

3) Subprocessors and limited access:
   - For on‑prem installs, the only potential subprocessors are (a) our third‑party installer partner for physical hardware shipments (name disclosed in DPA), and (b) an approved monitoring agent vendor if customer opts into managed observability.
   - Both are restricted to purpose‑limited access and only after POV signoff; remote access is disabled by default.

4) Data flows / cross‑border:
   - With fully private air‑gapped option: model weights, customer inputs, and logs do not leave your network. Aggregated telemetry (opt‑in) can be configured to send only anonymized counts to a regional endpoint.
   - If you want Redwood support to receive crash dumps or richer traces, that requires customer consent and is subject to SCCs / DPA clauses.

I'll inline some suggested technical language into the DPA doc for clarity. Happy to jump on a short call with Raj to walk through the break‑glass steps.

—Monica
Monica Patel
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Private deploy (VPC/on-prem) — DPA clauses and subprocessor commitments

Hi all — legal perspective and suggested DPA redlines. High level: we can meet MedTech's requirements for true customer‑controlled keys and restricted data flows for a private on‑prem installation. Key points to include in the DPA and SOW: 

- Key custody: explicit clause that customer retains exclusive control of the root/master key. Redwood will not require key escrow unless requested in writing; if escrow is requested it must be documented in the SOW with narrow access controls and a separate escrow agreement.

- Subprocessors: provide a short canonical list limited to (i) logistics/install partner, (ii) optional managed observability vendor, (iii) hosting partner for dedicated spare hardware (if relevant). Each subprocessor entry must include purpose, data categories accessible, and contact for audits. Any additions require 30 days notice and right to object.

- Operator access / break‑glass: define the narrow conditions under which operator access is permitted (safety/stability incident), require two‑party approval (customer security lead + Redwood legal), session recording, time‑boxed access, and post‑access forensic report. 

- Cross‑border / telemetry: commit that model artifacts and customer data remain in your network unless mutually agreed. Telemetry is opt‑in and limited to high‑level metrics; any transfer will rely on SCCs or equivalent protections.

- Audit & evidence: provide SOC2 attestation summary and offer an on‑site evidence review for top‑tier customers under NDA. We can add specific audit cadence in the SOW.

I'll attach redlines (see dpa_clause_suggestion.docx) and a short SOP for operator break‑glass. If MedTech needs additional contractual guarantees (e.g., no subprocessor in jurisdiction X), we can evaluate on a case‑by‑case basis.

Vivek Kulkarni
Head of Legal, Redwood Inference
